items.text: SEASON 1 · EPISODE 9 · DRAFT  Commissioning trial · Maya and Elias · Level L2 (Operator)  The new stage lighting works, and Elias still won't sign.  ⚑ RV-04 · RV-31: DMX and acceptance practice are simplified for teaching. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: Working Isn't Accepted
items.stakes: The donor's lighting works every Sunday. Elias won't sign, and the last payment waits on his signature.
items.reward: A signature that means something. Nico's first acceptance sheet.

objectives.text: Write a requirement Elias can sign against
Stop Nico swapping the wrong fixture
Look closer: two things that “worked for months”

items.rumor: At minute eleven, fixtures three to eight flicker. One and two never do.

items.alt: The stage under the new rig: eight fixtures on a truss, warm beams across the band's gear.
items.caption: Donor-funded. Installed in October. Beautiful. Not yet accepted.

items.alt: Nico, the vendor's installer in an orange polo, gestures proudly at the rig. Elias holds his clipboard.

bubbles.text: It's been working since October. Every Sunday.
Working and accepted aren't the same word. Where are the requirements?

lines.text: Working and accepted aren't the same word.

items.alt: Maya checks the folder the vendor left.

bubbles.text: There's a scope: “install eight fixtures, new DMX line, program looks.” That's it.
Then that's what we're doing first. Nobody signs a scope.

items.caption: The last payment waits on his signature.

items.prompt: Which of these is an acceptance requirement Elias can sign against?

options.label: “The lights should look good.”
options.consequence: No condition, no method, no threshold.
options.fail: A requirement nobody can fail is one nobody can pass.

options.label: “No visible flicker on any fixture during a 30-minute full-look run with the band playing, watched from FOH and on Cam 1 at 59.94p, 1/60. Pass = zero events.”
options.result: Elias writes it down word for word.
options.consequence: Requirement, condition, method, threshold — and it can fail.

options.label: “Fixtures must be high quality.”
options.consequence: An opinion about the product, not a claim about this install.

options.label: “It works every Sunday.”
options.result: Elias: “So does a lot of broken equipment.”

items.alt: The acceptance sheet, blank results so far: R1 addresses no overlap; R2 looks recall; R3 no flicker for 30 minutes at full with the band; R4 load within rating (Andre with a clamp meter); R5 no flicker on camera; R6 labeled drawing handed over.
items.caption: Six requirements. Each one can fail.

items.label: **Sequence:** put the acceptance work in order before Elias does.

items.alt: R1 test: Maya checks each fixture's address and footprint with a tester while Elias ticks.

bubbles.text: Fixture 6 starts at 81 and uses eighteen channels. Fixture 7 starts at 95.
Eighty-one to ninety-eight. So seven is sharing four of six's channels. Punch list, item one.

items.caption: R1 fails: an address overlap. Nobody noticed because the looks happened to hide it.

items.title: Nico's install notes
items.body: *addr fixt 7 = 95 (ran out of time to check).* Six words. The most important four are in brackets.

items.sub: Beginner · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Ray and Maya beside a board. DMX is how the console talks to lights: five hundred twelve channels on one line — a universe. Each fixture starts at its start address. Where does a fixture end? Start plus channels minus one. At a hundred one using sixteen channels, it ends at a hundred sixteen. The next fixture starts at a hundred seventeen.

bubbles.text: DMX is how the console talks to lights: five hundred twelve channels on one line — a universe. Each fixture starts at its start address.
Start plus channels minus one. At a hundred one using sixteen channels, it ends at a hundred sixteen. The next fixture starts at a hundred seventeen.

items.caption: Beginner: the term, what it means, the formula — and one worked example out loud.

items.text: 📘 RAY'S NOTEBOOK · BEGINNER  Terms    DMX   The control protocol for stage lighting: 512 channels per universe.   Universe   One DMX line of 512 channels.   Start address   The first DMX channel a fixture listens to.   Formula, variables and a worked example   ƒ FORMULA · Last channel a fixture uses  last = start + channels − 1   start  fixture start address  channels  channels the fixture uses    Worked example.  A fixture at 101 using 16 channels: 101 + 16 − 1 = 116.    ƒ FORMULA · Next free start address  next = start + channels   start  this fixture's start address  channels  channels it uses    Worked example.  A fixture at 101 using 16 channels: the next free address is 117.

📒 EMPATHIA LEARN FIELDBOOK · MODULE 10 OF 31 · PP. 155–159, 164–165  PART 10 LIGHTING ENGINEERING  Page 165, in Ray's handwriting: “One loose connector — every fixture after it. Check the chain in order, not the fixture you're mad at.”

items.label: **Fieldbook module 10 — Lighting basics and DMX addressing.** Beginner support: every new word is defined, and every formula comes with its variables and a worked example.

items.label: **Learn it now:** lighting control over networks — universes, nodes, RDM, and who owns the lighting network.

items.alt: The full-look run begins. Sofia, at the lighting console, brings every fixture to full while the band plays.
items.caption: R3 under the stated condition: full look, band playing, thirty minutes.

items.title: It isn't the fixture
items.body: Nico was sure fixture 3 was bad. Fixtures 1 and 2 are steady; 3 through 8 flicker together. The fault is at the link into fixture 3 — a microphone cable standing in for data cable — and the line has no terminator.

items.alt: Minute eleven: fixtures 3 through 8 start flickering at random. Fixtures 1 and 2 stay steady.
items.caption: Minute 11. Fixtures 3–8. Random.

items.alt: Nico is already heading for the door.

bubbles.text: Fixture three's bad. I've got a spare in the van — ten minutes.
Wait. Three through eight all flicker. One and two don't.

items.prompt: It's fixture three. I've got a spare in the van. Ten minutes and we're done. Come on.

options.label: “Three to eight all flicker. One and two don't. What sits between two and three?”
“Swap it. Worth a try.”
options.reply: Then we'll know nothing in ten minutes instead of something in two.

items.prompt: Nico wants to swap fixture 3. Elias leaves at 8:30. Decide.
items.happening: Fixtures 3–8 flicker at minute 11 of the run.
unknown: Where on the line the fault is
timeout: Nico goes to the van anyway and swaps fixture 3 while you're still thinking.
When you hesitate, somebody else's hunch becomes the plan.

hints.text: Everything downstream of a bad link inherits the fault.

options.label: Swap fixture 3
options.result: Ten minutes later: a new fixture 3. At minute 9 of a new run, 3 through 8 flicker again.
options.consequence: And the original fixture 3 is in the van, untested.
options.fail: Swapping parts on a hunch moves the problem and erases the evidence.

options.label: Stop. Tester at the console, then walk the line
options.result: Console output steady. Fixture 1 steady, 2 steady, 3 flickers. The fault is at or just upstream of fixture 3's input.
options.consequence: Ten minutes to the first failure point, with nothing changed.

options.label: Split the line with a Y-cable to “balance” it
options.consequence: DMX is a line, not a tree.
options.fail: You added a second fault to the first one.

options.label: Ask Elias to sign now; fix next week
options.result: Elias: “Sign what? I have a flicker and no cause.”
options.consequence: The answer is no, and he trusts you less.
options.fail: A signature is a claim about evidence. You had none.

items.label: **First failure point:** where on the line does the flicker start?

items.alt: Maya gently flexes the cable between fixtures 2 and 3. Fixture 3 stutters with every flex.
items.caption: Flex the link at the first failure point: fixture 3 stutters every time.

items.alt: System View: the DMX line from the console through fixtures 1 to 8. The link from 2 to 3 is marked red: a microphone-cable extension. Fixtures 3 to 8 flicker. Fixture 7's address overlaps fixture 6. There is no terminator at the end of the line.
items.caption: Three punch-list items on one line: the wrong cable, a missing terminator, an address overlap.

items.text: 🔭 PHYSICS IN MOTION  Mix Sofia's warm white  The science under this episode’s problem — live.

items.alt: Nico, holding the offending short cable, admits it.

bubbles.text: It was a short run. A mic cable fit, so I used it. It worked for months.
It worked until it didn't. That's why we run thirty minutes, not three.

lines.text: A mic cable fit, so I used it. It worked for months.
It worked until it didn't. That's the whole history of engineering in one sentence.

items.prompt: 8:02 p.m. Elias leaves at 8:30. The run takes thirty minutes. What now?
items.happening: Three faults found, twenty-eight minutes left.
timeout: 8:30 arrives with the fixes half done. Elias leaves; acceptance is rescheduled.
You knew what to do. Deciding late cost the day.
items.lab_label: fix all three punch-list items before Elias leaves.

options.label: Fix all three, rerun the failed test — full thirty minutes
options.result: Rated data cable on 2→3, a terminator at the end, fixture 7 readdressed to 99 and fixture 8 to 115. Rerun starts at 8:05.
options.consequence: It ends at 8:35. Elias looks at his watch — and stays.

options.label: Fix them, rerun for five minutes
options.consequence: The fault first showed at minute eleven. Five minutes proves nothing about it.
options.fail: A retest that ends before the original failure appeared isn't a retest.

options.label: Ask Elias to sign on a promise
Reschedule the whole acceptance
options.result: Safe, slow. Elias can come back in three weeks.
options.consequence: The donor payment slips a month. Nico's company is not pleased.

items.title: Three colors make them all
items.body: Thomas Young proposed in 1802 that the eye senses color with three receptors; Hermann von Helmholtz developed the idea. In 1861 James Clerk Maxwell used three filtered photographs — red, green, blue — to make the first color photograph, of a tartan ribbon.

items.alt: System View after the fix: rated data cable on every link, a terminator at the end of the line, fixture 7 readdressed to 99 and fixture 8 to 115. All eight fixtures green.
items.caption: Rated cable, a terminator, no overlaps.

items.alt: Minute eleven of the rerun. Every fixture steady. Elias watches without looking at his watch.
items.caption: Minute eleven comes and goes.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #10 · AVERY'S LENS  Define done in the user's terms  Acceptance criteria should describe what people will experience, with a way to measure it.  “No visible flicker for 30 minutes with the band playing, from FOH and on camera” is a promise to the audience, not a spec for a fixture.

items.alt: In the booth, Theo shows Camera 1 at 59.94p, 1/60 shutter: no flicker on any fixture.
items.caption: R5 on camera, the Christmas Eve settings.

items.alt: Minute thirty. The band finishes. Zero flicker events.
items.caption: Thirty minutes, full look, band playing: zero events.

items.alt: The completed acceptance sheet: all six requirements ticked, with methods and conditions, signed 'E.'
items.caption: Requirement, condition, method, result — and where the evidence lives.

items.title: Old sign-offs, clipped behind the new one
items.body: Other buildings, other years. One sheet is marked FAIL in red, then PASS six weeks later, then — in pencil, much later — *collapsed 2011, not our part.* He doesn't talk about that one.

items.alt: Elias signs and hands Maya a copy.

bubbles.text: Pass. Keep the evidence where the next person can find it.
Even the part where it failed?

items.alt: Elias answers, and Nico nods.

bubbles.text: Especially that. A pass that never failed tells you nothing about the test.
Nobody ever asked me for a sheet before.

lines.text: Nobody ever asked me for a sheet before.
Now somebody has. It gets easier. It never gets optional.

items.label: **Service Mode:** Elias is leaving in three minutes. Run the phantom flicker yourself.

items.text: 📁 CASE FILE · CASE-004 · from the Empathia Learn Fieldbook, pp. 164–165  Loose DMX: The Phantom Flicker  New stage lighting “works”. During acceptance, fixtures flicker at random.   Open the case file ▸   Learn · Service · Engineer — it doesn't change your story progress.

items.alt: Elias, leaving, gives one principle.

bubbles.text: A signature is a claim about evidence. Never sign anything you couldn't defend to a stranger.

items.alt: March. Ray, in row 12, voiceless with laryngitis, holds up a card: 'Laryngitis. Your booth today.'
items.caption: Next: *Sanctuary Blackout.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  “Works” is not “accepted.” Write requirements with a condition, a method and a threshold; test under the condition that matters; find the first failure point instead of swapping parts; rerun the failed test at least as long as it took to fail; record where the evidence lives.

REFLECTION (optional)  · Nico wasn't careless — nobody had ever asked him for proof. A good acceptance process is a kindness to the installer as well as the owner.  Boundary: this doesn't prove anything about the cable.
